blocks.text: 4. Nucleic acids and their building blocks

segments.text: , each composed of a nitrogenous base, a sugar (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA), and a phosphate group. In DNA, complementary bases on opposing strands pair via hydrogen bonding (adenine with thymine, guanine with cytosine) in a specific, predictable way that underlies both DNA’s stable double-helix structure and its ability to be accurately copied and read — the chemical basis of genetic information storage and transmission.

Across all four biomolecule classes, the same principle recurs: three-dimensional structure — determined by the underlying chemistry of bonding, hydrogen bonding, and stereochemistry covered throughout this Paper — directly enables biological function, whether that is an enzyme’s active site precisely recognising a substrate, a membrane’s bilayer separating cellular compartments, or DNA’s base-pairing enabling faithful genetic replication.

items.text: Carbohydrates range from single sugar units (monosaccharides) to large polymers (polysaccharides), with stereochemistry determining biological recognition.
Amino acids exist as zwitterions and link via peptide bonds into proteins, whose specific three-dimensional folding (not just their sequence) determines function.
Lipids’ dual polar/nonpolar character (especially in phospholipids) drives spontaneous bilayer formation, the structural basis of cell membranes.
Nucleic acids are nucleotide polymers whose specific, complementary base-pairing (in DNA) enables stable storage and accurate transmission of genetic information.
